title: Anaphylaxis
blurb: Recognise anaphylaxis, give the right IM adrenaline dose into the thigh, repeat it at 5 minutes, and manage fluids, refractory reactions, observation and follow-up.
question: Ms Petrova, 38, is 10 minutes into an IV antibiotic infusion on a surgical ward. She has a hoarse voice, wheeze, urticaria and a BP of 78/40. What should the nurse do first?

teach.body: Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening, generalised hypersensitivity reaction. RCUK recognition: sudden onset of Airway and/or Breathing and/or Circulation problems, usually with skin changes such as an itchy rash. Skin or mucosal changes on their own are not anaphylaxis, and skin changes can be absent. Plain English: if someone exposed to a trigger suddenly struggles to breathe or collapses, think anaphylaxis and give adrenaline; if in doubt, give it.
teach.cite: RCUK Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (May 2021, current); RCUK 2025 special circumstances

head: Look for
rows: Hoarse voice, stridor, throat or tongue swelling
Increased work of breathing, wheeze, fatigue, cyanosis, SpO2 below 94%
Low blood pressure, signs of shock, confusion, reduced consciousness
teach.caption: Medicines, especially antibiotics, and contrast media are common hospital triggers; foods and insect stings are common outside hospital.

steps.label: Remove trigger
steps.sub: e.g. stop the infusion; lie flat

steps.label: IM adrenaline
steps.sub: Anterolateral middle third of the thigh

steps.label: A, B, C support
steps.sub: High-flow oxygen; SpO2, ECG, BP monitoring

steps.label: No response at 5 min
steps.sub: Repeat IM adrenaline; IV fluid bolus

steps.label: No better after 2 doses
steps.sub: Refractory: confirm team called; follow refractory algorithm

head: Age
Dose
Volume
teach.caption: These doses are for IM injection only. IV adrenaline is given only by experienced specialists in an appropriate setting.

teach.body: Lie the person flat, with or without legs raised; sitting may ease breathing, with legs extended; if pregnant, lie on the left side. Never let them stand, walk or sit up suddenly during the reaction: fatal collapse can follow. If A, B or C problems persist after the first dose, give an IV crystalloid bolus: adults 500–1,000 mL, children 10 mL/kg, and give it early if there is shock.

teach.h: What helps, and what comes later

rows.label: Medicine
values: Non-sedating oral antihistamine for skin symptoms

rows.label: Not used for A, B, C

teach.caption: RCUK 2021: antihistamines must not delay adrenaline; non-sedating oral antihistamines are preferred to chlorphenamine; corticosteroids are no longer advised for routine emergency treatment.

head: Duration
When
rows: Good response within 5–10 min to one dose given within 30 min of onset; full resolution; has unused auto-injectors and training; supervised at home
Two doses of IM adrenaline needed, or previous biphasic reaction
More than 2 doses; severe asthma or severe respiratory compromise; continuing absorption; late at night; poor access to emergency care
teach.caption: Observe in an area able to treat life-threatening A, B, C problems. Before discharge, check for dizziness on standing.

items: Mast cell tryptase: first sample as soon as feasible without delaying treatment; second ideally 1–2 hours (no later than 4 hours) after onset; third at least 24 hours after resolution or at the allergy clinic.
Record the time of onset and the time of each sample on the form, tube and notes.
Refer everyone with suspected anaphylaxis to a specialist allergy clinic.
Offer an adrenaline auto-injector as an interim measure (unless the reaction was drug-induced), with training and an emergency action plan.
Report the reaction (including the Yellow Card scheme for medicines) and document the trigger as an allergy.

teach.h: Worked example: Ms Petrova on a surgical ward
items: She has airway (hoarse voice), breathing (wheeze) and circulation (BP 78/40) problems with urticaria: anaphylaxis.
The nurse stops the infusion, calls for help and lies her flat with her legs raised: despite the wheeze she is hypotensive, and RCUK keeps people with cardiovascular instability flat, not sitting up.
She gives adrenaline 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL) IM into the anterolateral thigh, then high-flow oxygen and monitoring.
At 5 minutes there is no improvement: a second IM dose and a 500–1,000 mL crystalloid bolus are given. She improves; tryptase samples are timed and she is observed for at least 6 hours.

teach.text: 1 in 1,000 (1 mg/mL) is the IM strength: an adult dose is 0.5 mL. Do not reach for chlorphenamine or hydrocortisone first: they do not treat airway, breathing or circulation problems, and adrenaline must never wait for them.

items: Sudden A, B or C problems, usually with skin changes: think anaphylaxis; skin changes alone are not.
IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL into the anterolateral thigh: 500 / 300 / 150 / 100–150 micrograms by age.
Repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement; IV fluid bolus (adults 500–1,000 mL, children 10 mL/kg).
Refractory: no better after two IM doses; antihistamines third line; steroids not routine.
Observe 2, 6 or 12 hours by risk; timed tryptase; allergy referral and auto-injector training.

summary: You can now recognise anaphylaxis from its airway, breathing and circulation features, give the correct IM adrenaline dose for any age, repeat it at 5 minutes and give IV fluids. You know what refractory anaphylaxis means, why antihistamines and steroids are not first line, and how to observe, sample and refer afterwards.

A.q: Lily, 4, develops stridor and facial swelling after eating at a hospital outpatient clinic. What IM adrenaline dose does the RCUK algorithm give for her age?
A.why: RCUK: children aged 6 months to 6 years receive 150 micrograms IM (0.15 mL of 1 mg/mL adrenaline).

whyNot.0: 300 micrograms is the dose for children aged 6–12 years.
whyNot.1: 500 micrograms is the dose for adults and children over 12.
whyNot.3: 1 mL of 1 mg/mL would be 1,000 micrograms; 100–150 micrograms is for infants under 6 months.

A.q: Mr Hale, 50, develops an itchy urticarial rash 20 minutes after starting an oral antibiotic. His airway, breathing and blood pressure are normal. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: Not anaphylaxis by itself; watch for A, B, C problems
Anaphylaxis, so IM adrenaline is needed now
Not anaphylaxis, so the antibiotic can continue
A.why: RCUK: skin or mucosal changes alone are not a sign of anaphylaxis. He needs close monitoring for airway, breathing or circulation problems, and the suspected trigger should be reviewed.

whyNot.0: Urticaria without A, B or C problems does not meet the definition.
whyNot.2: IM adrenaline is for anaphylaxis with A, B or C problems; these are absent.
whyNot.3: A reaction to the antibiotic still needs the prescriber to review it; it should not simply continue.

A.q: Mr Ross, 60, has anaphylaxis with a BP of 80/50. After his first dose of IM adrenaline he says he needs the toilet and tries to get up. What should the nurse do?
options: Help him walk to the toilet with support
Sit him fully upright in a chair
Keep him lying flat, legs raised if possible
Stand him up briefly to check for dizziness
A.why: RCUK: fatality can occur within minutes if a patient stands, walks or sits up suddenly; patients must not walk or stand during acute reactions. Keep him supine, with legs raised if possible.

whyNot.0: Walking during a reaction with hypotension can cause fatal collapse.
whyNot.1: Sitting fully upright with low blood pressure risks collapse; sitting is only for breathing difficulty.
whyNot.3: The stand-up check is done before discharge, not during the acute reaction.

B.q: Ms Okoro, 29, has been stabilised after anaphylaxis but still has itchy urticaria. Which treatment does RCUK guidance prefer for these persisting skin symptoms?
options: A third dose of IM adrenaline
B.why: RCUK 2021: non-sedating oral antihistamines, in preference to chlorphenamine, may be given after initial stabilisation, especially for persisting skin symptoms.

whyNot.0: Chlorphenamine causes sedation and is not preferred.
whyNot.1: Adrenaline treats A, B or C problems; persisting skin symptoms do not need more.
whyNot.2: Corticosteroids are no longer advised for routine emergency treatment of anaphylaxis.

B.q: Mrs Daley, 55, remains hypotensive 5 minutes after her first IM adrenaline dose. A second dose is given. What IV fluid bolus does the RCUK algorithm describe for an adult?
B.why: RCUK anaphylaxis algorithm: IV fluid challenge with crystalloid, adults 500–1,000 mL, children 10 mL/kg.

whyNot.1: 250 mL is the NICE NG253 sepsis bolus, not the anaphylaxis adult volume.
whyNot.3: RCUK uses crystalloid, and 2,000 mL is not the stated bolus.

B.q: Mr Tan, 41, needed two doses of IM adrenaline for anaphylaxis and his symptoms have now resolved. He has no other risk factors. What is the recommended minimum observation?
options: At least 6 hours after symptoms resolve
24 hours from the first dose given
B.why: RCUK 2021: a minimum of 6 hours' observation after resolution is recommended when two doses of IM adrenaline were needed (or after a previous biphasic reaction).

whyNot.0: Fast-track after 2 hours needs a good response to a single dose; he needed two.
whyNot.2: 12 hours applies to more than two doses or other high-risk features he does not have.
whyNot.3: 24 hours is not one of the RCUK observation categories.

C.q: Mrs Ibrahim, 66, has had two correctly given IM adrenaline doses for anaphylaxis 5 minutes apart and an IV fluid bolus. She remains wheezy with a BP of 74/40. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Confirm the team is coming; refractory algorithm
Give 1 mg of adrenaline IV as a bolus
Sit her up and wait 30 minutes for a response
C.why: RCUK: no improvement in breathing or circulation despite two appropriate IM doses is refractory anaphylaxis. Confirm the resuscitation team or ambulance has been called and follow the refractory algorithm, where specialists give IV adrenaline.

whyNot.1: A 1 mg IV bolus is a cardiac arrest dose; IV adrenaline for anaphylaxis is given only by experienced specialists, usually as an infusion.
whyNot.2: Antihistamines and steroids do not treat refractory airway, breathing or circulation problems.
whyNot.3: Sitting up with hypotension risks collapse, and waiting delays specialist treatment.

C.q: Ms Petrova's anaphylaxis began at 10:10 and a first tryptase sample was taken at 10:30 after treatment. When should the second sample ideally be taken?
options: Once she has been discharged home
1–2 hours after the onset of symptoms
C.why: RCUK 2021: ideally take a second sample 1–2 hours (and no later than 4 hours) after onset, when tryptase usually peaks, and a third at least 24 hours after resolution.

whyNot.0: Sampling must never delay treatment, and tryptase may not rise for 30 minutes or more.
whyNot.1: 48 hours describes the baseline sample (at least 24 hours after resolution), not the second.
whyNot.2: Waiting until discharge misses the peak, which is 1–2 hours after onset.

C.q: Mr Ward, 22, is ready for discharge after anaphylaxis to peanuts. Which plan follows RCUK and NICE guidance?
options: Allergy clinic referral; auto-injector and training
GP review if symptoms come back at home
A 5-day course of oral steroids and no referral
Carry chlorphenamine in place of adrenaline
C.why: All patients should be referred to a specialist allergy clinic and offered an adrenaline injector as an interim measure (unless drug-induced), with training and an emergency action plan.

whyNot.1: Waiting for recurrence leaves him without an auto-injector or specialist assessment.
whyNot.2: Steroids are not routine and do not replace allergy referral.
whyNot.3: Antihistamines do not treat anaphylaxis; adrenaline is the treatment.

reteach.title: The thigh, the dose, the clock
reteach.question: Anaphylaxis treatment comes down to three things. Can you name them?

blocks.body: The thigh: IM into the anterolateral middle third. The dose: 1 mg/mL adrenaline, 0.5 mL for an adult or child over 12, less for younger children. The clock: if there is no improvement after 5 minutes, give it again and start IV fluids. Two doses and still struggling? That is refractory anaphylaxis: specialist help now.

items.label: Call help, remove trigger, IM adrenaline
No better: second IM dose, IV fluids

blocks.text: The volume matches the dose only at 1 mg/mL: 500 micrograms = 0.5 mL, 300 = 0.3 mL, 150 = 0.15 mL.

explain.body: Sudden Airway (hoarse voice, stridor), Breathing (wheeze, increased work, cyanosis, SpO2 below 94%) or Circulation (hypotension, shock, confusion) problems, usually with skin changes.

test.q: Which finding is listed by RCUK as a life-threatening Breathing problem in anaphylaxis?
test.why: RCUK lists increased work of breathing, wheeze, fatigue, cyanosis and SpO2 below 94% as breathing problems.

whyNot.1: A rash is a skin change, not a breathing problem.
whyNot.2: Eyelid swelling is a mucosal or skin change.
whyNot.3: Nausea is not one of the life-threatening A, B, C features.

explain.body: 1 mg/mL (1 in 1,000) adrenaline IM into the anterolateral middle third of the thigh: 0.5 mL for adults and children over 12.

test.q: What volume of 1 mg/mL adrenaline is given IM to an adult with anaphylaxis?
test.why: 500 micrograms of 1 mg/mL adrenaline is 0.5 mL.

whyNot.0: 0.3 mL (300 micrograms) is for children aged 6–12.
whyNot.1: 5 mL would be 5 mg, a dangerous overdose.
whyNot.2: 0.15 mL (150 micrograms) is for children aged 6 months to 6 years.

explain.body: If A, B or C problems persist, repeat IM adrenaline after 5 minutes and give an IV fluid bolus. No improvement despite two appropriate IM doses is refractory anaphylaxis.

test.q: If anaphylaxis has not improved, how long after the first IM adrenaline dose should it be repeated?
test.why: RCUK: repeat IM adrenaline after 5 minutes if airway, breathing or circulation problems persist.

whyNot.0: 15 minutes leaves life-threatening problems untreated too long.
whyNot.1: 30 minutes is far too long to wait.
whyNot.3: One minute is too soon to judge the response; RCUK uses 5 minutes.

explain.body: Antihistamines are third line and not for A, B, C problems; corticosteroids are not routine. After stabilisation, a non-sedating oral antihistamine may help skin symptoms.

test.q: What is the current RCUK position on corticosteroids such as hydrocortisone in the emergency treatment of anaphylaxis?
options: They are no longer routinely advised
Give them in place of a second dose
They are the treatment for refractory cases
test.why: RCUK 2021: corticosteroids are no longer advised for the routine emergency treatment of anaphylaxis.

whyNot.0: Nothing should delay adrenaline, the first-line treatment.
whyNot.2: A second IM adrenaline dose is the treatment if there is no improvement.
whyNot.3: Refractory anaphylaxis is treated with specialist IV adrenaline, not steroids.
